new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is on the last syllable of the word ('generally'), so stress is predictable and non-contrastive; stressed vs unstressed position conditions vowel allophony (ATR advancement of high vowels and schwa in stressed syllables).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets seen.
new_statements.exceptions: The hedge 'generally' implies exceptions, but none are visible in the snippets; the book's 'Suprasegmentals' section (not seen) may qualify the rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('word stress'); citation forms presumably. Snippet spacing normalized (Google renders '/ ४ /' for /u/ and puts spaces around punctuation); the sentence boundaries are Google's.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress statement is from Sudarsono's 'Bakatik Dayak language', which he describes as having c. 60,000 speakers in West Kalimantan (i.e. Bakatik broadly). Glottolog files Sudarsono 2002 and Azharie 2001 under beka1241 (Riuk Bekati', ISO bei), but a 2009 Anthropologica snippet calls Sudarsono's thesis one 'on Bekati' (Lara')', and the catalogue descriptions of Azharie 2001 and Hanye 1988 say their Bakatik is that of the Dayak Lara people of Kabupaten Sambas; the Lara/Rara variety has its own glottocode rara1235 (Rara Bakati', ISO lra). Which dialect(s) the 2013 phonology covers is not visible in the snippets.

new_statements.quote: [p. 292] From rather early in this exploration of the full/reduced contrast it seemed that such a contrast could have arisen from differences of accentual patterns at an earlier stage even though an accentual difference is not evident in the contemporary Land Dayak languages. They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position. [p. 47] In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually). [...] In some words of the shape (C)V.V(C), in western dialects (Singai, Jagoi) and also in Rara, the same vowel occurs in both the ultima (last syllable) and the penult (second-to-last syllable). In such words initiation of stress (accent) on the ultima vowel is usually perceptible: (C)V1.ˈV1(C).

new_statements.relation_note: Final-syllable placement matches the catalog record (final stress = final) and Sudarsono 2013's 'Word stress in Bakatik generally falls on the word-final syllable. Thus, it is not phonemic.' The book's statement is at the Land Dayak group level (explicitly including the Bakati' cluster: Rara, Sara/Riok, Kendayan, Bekati'), plus a Rara-specific phonetic remark; it adds the detail that stress is most evident utterance-finally/in citation forms and that there is no accentual contrast. The 'Bekati'' data in the book are Hudson's (1970) wordlist of unknown location (fn. 48, p. 211); the Rara data are from Lundu District, Sarawak, plus Bryant 1990 (Lara', Sara/Riok, Kendayan, West Kalimantan).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress/accent falls consistently on the final syllable (ultima) of the stem in all contemporary Land Dayak languages, a group the book defines as Bidayuh + Bakati' (Rara, Sara/Riok, Kendayan, Bekati') + Southern Land Dayak; most evident utterance-finally and in citation forms. For Rara (a Bakati' variety) specifically, stress onset on the ultima is perceptible even in (C)V.V(C) words with identical vowels. No accentual contrast exists; earlier PAN accent differences survive only as full vs. reduced penult vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Hedges: 'at least in citation forms' and 'perhaps in context' (fn. 79, p. 94: a post-clitic takes the stress placement of the word it attaches to, since word stress is final). The Proto Bakati' chapter (Part III sec. 3, pp. 211-231) contains no stress statement of its own.
new_statements.identity_note: Rensch et al. 2012 treat 'Bakati'' as a cluster of four closely related languages: Rara (Lundu District, Sarawak, and around Bengkayang, West Kalimantan; Bryant's 'Lara''), Sara/Riok, Kendayan (near Ledo) and 'Bekati'' (Hudson 1970 wordlist, location unknown). Glottolog beka1241 is Riuk Bekati' (ISO bei); Sudarsono's 'Bakatik' (the catalog source) covers the Riuk, Sara and Lara dialects together. Rensch's group-level stress statement (p. 292) therefore covers beka1241 by inclusion; the only variety-specific stress remark (p. 47) names Rara, which Glottolog files separately as Rara Bakati' (lara1264) but which Sudarsono counts as a dialect of Bakatik.
